props.title: Once Upon a Time in America
props.initialSlug: Epic tale of friendship, crime, and betrayal in NYC

sections.content: Sergio Leone's epic Once Upon a Time in America stands as the ultimate meditation on memory, time, and the dark underbelly of the American Dream. Like Leone's masterful The Good, the Bad and the Ugly (1966), it shatters conventional narrative structure, weaving between 1920s, 1930s and 1960s New York with dreamlike fluidity. The film's approach to chronology influenced later works like Pulp Fiction (1994) and The Godfather Part II (1974), showing how personal and criminal histories intertwine across decades. movies.title: Once Upon a Time in America
movies.slug: Leone's 229-minute gangster epic following Jewish criminals across 40 years of NYC history

sections.content: Robert De Niro's haunting performance as Noodles anchors the film's exploration of guilt, betrayal and lost innocence. The controversial rape scenes and unflinching violence serve Leone's broader commentary on how America's promise of prosperity often comes through brutal means. This theme of violence underlying "legitimate" society appears in later films like Casino (1995) and Road to Perdition (2002), though few match Leone's operatic scope.

The film's innovative sound design, featuring Ennio Morricone's haunting score and strategic use of "Amapola," creates a hypnotic atmosphere that enhances its dream-like quality. This technique influenced later crime epics like The Untouchables (1987) and Once Upon a Time in Hollywood (2019), where music becomes crucial to period authenticity and emotional resonance. movies.title: Goodfellas
movies.slug: Scorsese's kinetic adaptation of Henry Hill's mob life spanning three decades

sections.content: The film's restored 229-minute version reveals Leone's complete vision, demonstrating how extended runtime can create an immersive historical experience. This approach influenced modern epics like The Irishman (2019) and Gangs of New York (2002), which similarly use length to explore how criminal enterprises shaped American cities. The film's meditation on time and memory created a template for nonlinear crime narratives like Carlito's Way (1993) and A Most Violent Year (2014).
